d: From a fresh VPS to a Laravel app on HTTPS in five commands.
x: From a fresh Ubuntu server to a Laravel app on HTTPS, in about fifteen minutes. Every step shows the real command and what it prints; click a terminal to jump to the end. Install one command on the server Log in as cipi, with your SSH key Create an app isolated user, DB, PHP Deploy zero downtime from Git HTTPS Let's Encrypt, auto-renewed You need: an Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 VPS with a public IP, a domain whose DNS you control, and a Git repository. Cipi is free; the only cost is the server. 1. Install Cipi SSH into the fresh server as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer. It asks for your

SSH into the fresh server as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer. It asks for your SSH public key, shows its plan, then installs and hardens the whole stack. $ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash Save the credentials it prints. Requirements, SSH keys and unattended installs: Install Cipi .
Root login over SSH is now off. Connect as cipi with your key and prefix commands with sudo (no password needed for cipi ). $ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10 $ sudo cipi status

The wizard asks for the app type, runtime, database, name, domain and repository, then builds an isolated app: its own Linux user, database, PHP pool, Nginx vhost, worker and deploy key. $ sudo cipi app create Skip the questions with flags: sudo cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --branch=main The summary at the end (database password, deploy key, webhook token, a mariadb+ssh:// URL for TablePlus or DBeaver) is shown once . Save it.

If you gave the installer a Git token, there is nothing to do: Cipi added the deploy key and the push webhook to the repository. Otherwise add the ssh-ed25519 … key from the summary as a read-only deploy key : Provider Where GitHub Repository → Settings → Deploy keys GitLab Settings → Repository → Deploy keys Bitbucket Repository settings → Access keys Azure DevOps User settings → SSH public keys Then check that the server can read it: sudo cipi git check myapp . Tokens and automatic setup: Git providers .

Cipi keeps cache, sessions and queues in each app's own database , so no app can read another's data. Laravel 11+ ships those tables; on an older project create them once and commit: php artisan cache:table && php artisan session:table && php artisan queue:table Migrations run on every deploy. Prefer Valkey for speed or Horizon? Switch per app in Valkey .

$ sudo cipi deploy myapp The new release is built in its own folder, migrated, then made live with one atomic symlink swap. Visitors never see a half-deployed app, and cipi deploy myapp --rollback goes back in a second. How it works: Deploy & roll back .

Point the domain's DNS at the server, then: $ sudo cipi ssl install myapp The certificate covers the domain and its aliases and renews itself. Behind the Cloudflare proxy use --dns=cloudflare and set SSL/TLS to Full (strict) . More in SSL certificates .

Prefer a browser, or need one for clients? Install the API and the panel, each on its own domain. The panel can manage this server and any other Cipi server you connect. $ sudo cipi api api.example.com $ sudo cipi gui panel.example.com

d: The stack Cipi installs and how each app is laid out on disk.
x: Cipi is a command-line tool that lives on your server. It installs a proven open-source stack, then creates and runs apps on it, each one sealed off from the others. There is no external service in the loop: no account, no agent phoning home, nothing to pay. The server Nginx web server, TLS, proxy PHP-FPM / Octane several PHP versions side by side MariaDB / PostgreSQL one database per app Valkey cache, queues (opt-in per app) Supervisor workers, Horizon, Reverb Component Role Nginx (nginx.org mainline) Web server, reverse proxy, TLS termination, HTTP/2 hardening PHP-FPM PHP runtime per app; 8.

d: Run apps on FrankenPHP, convert existing apps and pin builds.
x: Laravel Octane keeps your app booted in memory and serves requests with FrankenPHP. Typical result: much lower response times for the same hardware. Octane and PHP-FPM apps run side by side on one server. Create or convert Your repository needs laravel/octane , installed with php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp . Octane starts after the first deploy. cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --octane cipi app convert myapp --to=octane # an existing FPM app cipi app convert myapp --to=fpm # and back cipi app limits myapp --octane-work

Your repository needs laravel/octane , installed with php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp . Octane starts after the first deploy. cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --octane cipi app convert myapp --to=octane # an existing FPM app cipi app convert myapp --to=fpm # and back cipi app limits myapp --octane-workers=4

Nginx static files, proxy to Octane Octane on 127.0.0.1 port 8100–8999 FrankenPHP build pinned per app Supervisor keeps it running, reloads on deploy Piece Setting Nginx proxy_pass to the app's local port; static files from current/public ; no PHP-FPM pool Process Supervisor program myapp-octane , next to the queue workers Deploys The pinned FrankenPHP binary is linked into each release, then Octane reloads .env OCTANE_SERVER=frankenphp , OCTANE_HTTPS=true Converting rewrites the vhost, process, deploy recipe and .env , and keeps the certificate. It turns JIT off; enable it again if you use it.

The PHP an Octane app runs is the one compiled into its FrankenPHP binary. Cipi keeps those binaries in /opt/cipi-frankenphp/builds/ (read-only to apps) and pins one per app . A deploy never downloads a new binary, so PHP changes only when you decide. cipi frankenphp # each app's build and PHP, patched or not cipi frankenphp upgrade myapp # newest build on the same PHP minor cipi frankenphp upgrade --all cipi frankenphp use myapp # pin a specific build cipi frankenphp import ./frankenphp # a build you compiled (other PHP minor) cipi frankenphp adopt myapp # pin the binary Octane downloaded cipi frankenphp prune # remove unused builds Rule Why it keeps you stable Upgrades stay on the app's PHP minor and FrankenPHP major No surprise PHP 8.5 → 8.6 jump Octane must answer after an upgrade, or the previous build returns A bad build never stays live A deploy that needs a newer FrankenPHP stops before migrations The live release is untouched; run cipi frankenphp upgrade Apps on different PHP minors use different builds 8.5 and 8.6 coexist Nightly patches via cipi autoupdate (component frankenphp ) Security fixes without manual work To move an app to a new PHP minor: cipi app edit myapp --php=8.6 , then cipi frankenphp upgrade myapp . Octane serves HTTP only. Run long jobs on queue workers or Horizon and WebSockets on Reverb .

d: Turn the OPcache JIT on or off for a single app.
x: PHP's JIT compiles hot code to machine code. It helps CPU-bound work (calculations, big collections, heavy templating) and does little for requests that mostly wait on the database. Cipi turns it on for one app , FPM or Octane, and checks it before and after. cipi app jit myapp on # tracing mode, 128M buffer cipi app jit myapp on --mode=function --buffer=256M cipi app jit myapp off cipi app jit myapp --json # current state Check When If it fails PHP can start with JIT (no Xdebug/pcov, JIT compiled in) Before Refused, nothing written PHP-FPM active / Octane answering After Previous setting rest

d: SPA, static and SSR frontends built on every deploy.
x: Node apps build and serve modern front-ends with the same lifecycle as Laravel apps: releases, rollback, webhook, SSL, basic auth, redirects, proxies and the deploy audit. # Vite SPA: build, serve dist/ with an index.html fallback cipi app create --user=web --domain=web.example.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/web.git --node=spa --framework=vite # Pre-rendered site (Astro, Nuxt generate, Next export) cipi app create --user=docs --domain=docs.example.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/docs.git --node=static --output=dist # Node server with blue/green deploys cipi app create --user=shop

Mode Nginx Use for spa Serves the build; unknown paths fall back to /index.html Client-side routed apps static Serves the build; real 404s via /404.html Pre-rendered sites ssr Proxies to a Node process on localhost, WebSockets included Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Remix, Astro SSR Hashed assets ( assets/ , _astro/ , _nuxt/ , _app/immutable/ ) are cached as immutable; HTML is never cached.

Flag Meaning --framework Preset: vite (spa), next , nuxt , sveltekit , astro , remix (ssr). Explicit flags win --node-version LTS major: 22 or 24 (default: the server default ) --build Build command (default npm run build ) --start SSR start command, a Node runner plus arguments, e.g. node build --output Build folder for spa/static; the deploy fails if it has no index.html --health-path SSR path that must answer below 500 before a release takes traffic (default / ) The build installs from your lockfile ( npm ci , pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , yarn install --immutable , bun install --frozen-lockfile ) with NODE_ENV=production . shared/.env is read at build time and by SSR servers at runtime; edit it with cipi app env .

Start new release on the idle slot Health check must answer < 500 in 60 s Switch upstream nginx -t, reload Drain old slot then stop it Two Supervisor programs ( shop-node-blue , shop-node-green ) each own a local port. If the new release crashes or never answers, it is stopped, the old slot keeps serving and the deploy fails before anything goes live. Rollback and cipi node restart switch the same way. The switch runs as root through a narrow rule: ports, start command, Node version and health path come from a root-owned file, not from the app. .env is read as data, never executed; HOST is forced to 127.0.0.1 and the start command runs without a shell.

cipi node status shop # mode, commands, slots cipi node restart shop # zero downtime cipi node logs shop --lines=100 cipi app edit shop --start="node .output/server/index.mjs" --health-path=/health cipi app edit web --node=static --output=dist The same settings can live in your repository in the node: section of cipi.yml . Push-to-deploy works without a Laravel agent: Cipi ships a hardened webhook receiver that verifies GitHub/Bitbucket signatures and GitLab/Azure tokens. Node apps get no database by default; add one with cipi db . cipi sync and cipi app clone do not handle Node apps yet.

cipi worker horizon enable myapp cipi worker horizon status myapp cipi worker horizon disable myapp Horizon replaces the queue:work workers of that app (one or the other, not both). It needs the queues on Redis: set QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis with cipi app env ; each app has its own Valkey instance ready. When a deploy finds laravel/horizon installed, it helps without overriding your choices: The deploy finds It does Horizon, queues on Redis, no worker Enables Horizon Horizon plus existing workers Explains how to switch; changes nothing Horizon, queues not on Redis Tells you which variable to set A Horizon you disabled stays disabled. cipi pending lists apps with Horizon installed but nothing processing jobs.

Stop workers before the symlink swap Swap release atomic Restart workers on the new code Workers never run old code against a new database. Supervisor restarts a worker only after an unexpected exit. Workers can also be declared in cipi.yml .
App users manage their own workers without root, through a narrow helper: sudo cipi-worker status myapp sudo cipi-worker restart myapp

d: The Laravel scheduler and each app user's crontab.

Nginx is excluded from unattended upgrades so it never restarts unexpectedly. When a new minor comes out, the extension packages ( redis , memcached , imagick ) follow a few days later. Cipi handles the gap: Situation Cipi PHP packaged, some extensions not yet Installs it, records what's missing, adds each extension as soon as it's published (nightly) Only a release candidate available Installs it and labels it prerelease Assigning a version still missing extensions Refused with the list of what's missing; --force if the app doesn't use them A lock file that rejects the new PHP The deploy fails and the live release stays: update the dependency, commit, deploy

PHP is excluded from Ubuntu's unattended upgrades: Cipi patches it itself every night at 03:30 , restarts only the affected PHP-FPM services and reports the result. cipi php upgrade # patch now and print the patch level State Meaning patched At or past the latest security release Cipi knows VULNERABLE A fix exists but isn't installed yet (exit code 1; the nightly job alerts until fixed) distro Ubuntu build: fixes backported without a version bump END OF LIFE No more fixes from PHP: move apps off it prerelease Release candidate, not compared Octane apps run the PHP inside their FrankenPHP binary, which apt never touches; cipi php upgrade lists them too and cipi frankenphp upgrade fixes them.

Every pool Cipi writes (apps, webhook receivers, panel) locks down settings that recent PHP advisories used as attack paths, and Octane apps load the same rules: php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off php_admin_flag[fatal_error_backtraces] = off They are set as admin flags, so neither .user.ini nor ini_set() can turn them back on. The API runs as www-data and calls cipi through /etc/sudoers.d/cipi-api , an explicit allowlist of subcommands with their exact argument shapes, checked with visudo -cf whenever a migration regenerates it. Vault and MariaDB credentials stay inside Cipi, never in PHP. Its FPM pool has its own open_basedir . Restrict REST and MCP clients by source IP. /etc/cipi/api-ip-whitelist holds one IPv4/IPv6 address or CIDR per line; * or no file allows all. The file is replaced atomically.

d: Manage your servers from your own terminal, without SSH.
x: cipi-cli manages your Cipi servers from your laptop, without SSH . It's a single Go binary (Linux and macOS, amd64 and arm64, MIT) that talks to each server's Cipi API : apps, deploys, cipi.yml , SSL, databases and anonymized dumps, PHP, services, keys, SMTP, health checks and disk usage. One profile per server, so a fleet is one command away. $ cipi-cli api token add prod $ cipi-cli status $ cipi-cli staging deploy myapp Each server needs cipi api installed, and a token from cipi api token create . Install chmod +x cipi-cli-* && sudo mv cipi-cli-* /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli # from GitHub Release

chmod +x cipi-cli-* && sudo mv cipi-cli-* /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli # from GitHub Releases cipi-cli version Binaries ship with SHA-256 checksums on GitHub Releases . From source: git clone https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli && cd cli && make build && sudo make install .

A profile is one server: API endpoint plus token, stored in ~/.cipi/config.json (mode 0600 ). cipi-cli api token add prod Cipi API endpoint: https://api.example.com API token: 1|yourtoken... Server profile "prod" saved → ~/.cipi/config.json cipi-cli profiles add staging --endpoint https://api.staging.example.com --token "1|…"

Prefix any command with a profile to target that server, or set a default. cipi-cli prod deploy shop cipi-cli profiles use prod cipi-cli apps list # uses prod cipi-cli staging apps list # an explicit prefix still wins Command Does profiles / profiles list List servers (alias servers ) profiles add <name> Add or update ( --endpoint , --token ) profiles show [name] One profile, token masked, or all profiles use <name> Default server profiles delete <name> Local credentials only; nothing changes on the server

Command Does apps list , apps show <app> List, details (environment included) apps create [flags] Create; prints credentials, deploy key and whether the key can read the repository apps edit <app> [flags] PHP, repository, branch, environment, domain, Node settings apps delete <app> [-y] Delete apps suspend , unsuspend <app> 503 maintenance page, without deleting apps logs <app> [--type --page --per-page] nginx, php, laravel, worker, deploy; page 1 is newest apps artisan <app> <cmd> Artisan as an async job apps run <app> <cmd> Allowlisted binaries ( cipi-cli run-commands ) `apps env show set <app>` Read .env , or --set KEY=VALUE / --unset KEY `apps auth show create update delete <app>` Composer auth.json `apps basicauth status enable disable <app>` HTTP Basic Auth `apps node status restart <app>` Node status, blue/green restart `apps search enable disable <app>` Meilisearch for one app apps webhook recreate <app> [--rotate-secret] New Git webhook, optionally a new secret apps fix-permissions <app> Restore home permissions Create flag Meaning --user , --domain App name (Linux user, database), primary domain --repository , --branch Git source --php e.g. 8.6 --env Environment label; picks cipi-<env>.yml --engine mariadb or pgsql --octane true / frankenphp --node-build Asset build on every deploy, e.g. npm ci && npm run build --custom , --docroot Non-Laravel app --node , --framework , --node-version , --build , --start , --output , --health-path Node apps cipi-cli apps create --user=shop --domain=shop.com --php=8.6 \ --repository=git@github.com:acme/shop.git --branch=main --node

Command Does deploy <app> Zero-downtime deploy, waits for the job deploy rollback <app> [-y] Previous release deploy unlock <app> Clear a stuck lock `deploy config show set <app>` deploy.php options: --optimize , --storage-link , --queue-restart , --horizon-terminate , --predeploy-snapshot , --node-build , --extra-artisan deploy audit <app> [--days N] Deploy ledger : origin, operator, IP, commit yml <app> The live cipi.yml : file, environment, validity, what applying would change yml apply <app> Apply it as a job `yml auto <app> on off status` Apply after every deploy (asks for confirmation) cipi-cli deploy shop Deploying shop... With auto-apply on, anyone who can push can change the app's server settings: that's the point, and the reason it asks first.

The CLI reads APP_URL and the anonymizer token from the app's .env through the API and calls the agent on the app. The signed link arrives by e-mail and lasts 15 minutes. cipi-cli apps artisan shop cipi:service anonymize --enable cipi-cli apps artisan shop cipi:generate-token anonymize cipi-cli apps artisan shop cipi:init-anonymize cipi-cli prod db anonymize shop --email dev@example.com ✓ Anonymization job queued for 'shop' cipi-cli db anonymize download "<signed url>" -o - | mysql -u root shop_local Flags: --email , --url (when the app redirects, redirects are never followed), --token , -o , --force . d: cipi/sdk for Laravel and any PHP app.
x: cipi/sdk is the PHP client for the Cipi API . From a Laravel app, a Symfony service or a plain script, one token calls the same surface as cipi-cli and the web panel : apps, deploys, cipi.yml , domains, databases, backups and the server. It runs on your machine over HTTPS: no SSH, no shelling out to cipi . composer require cipi/sdk PHP 8.2+ with ext-curl and ext-json ; Laravel optional. Source: github.com/cipi-sh/sdk (MIT). The server needs cipi api and a token with only the abilities this code needs. Client use Cipi\Sdk\Cipi; $cipi = Cipi::connect( baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com', // "/api

use Cipi\Sdk\Cipi; $cipi = Cipi::connect( baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com', // "/api" suffix optional token: getenv('CIPI_TOKEN') ?: '', ); $apps = $cipi->apps()->list(); $job = $cipi->deploys()->start('shop'); // 202 + job_id $done = $cipi->wait($job); // polls until completed or failed Reads return the JSON body as an array; writes return a job you can wait() on. Plain http:// is refused unless you pass ['allow_http' => true] (for a local panel).

Auto-discovered on Laravel 11, 12 and 13. php artisan vendor:publish --tag=cipi-config CIPI_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com CIPI_TOKEN= CIPI_TIMEOUT=30 use Cipi\Sdk\Laravel\Facades\Cipi; Cipi::apps()->list(); Or type-hint Cipi\Sdk\Cipi . The container holds one server; for another, call Cipi::connect() with its URL and token. Symfony and others register Cipi::connect() in their own container. Install it next to cipi/agent and the app's MCP server gains panel tools: panel_rollback , panel_deploy_audit , panel_db_backup , panel_job , panel_status .

Invalid values throw ValidationException (422). $cipi->wait($cipi->deploys()->start('shop')); $cipi->deploys()->rollback('shop'); $cipi->deploys()->unlock('shop'); $cipi->deploys()->audit('shop', days: 30); $cipi->deploys()->status('shop', tail: 50); // running, queued, interrupted, idle $cipi->deploys()->history('shop', limit: 10); $cipi->deploys()->last(); // last run of every app $cipi->deployConfig()->update('shop', ['keep_releases' => 5, 'migrate' => true]); $cipi->jobs()->wait($job, timeoutSeconds: 120, intervalSeconds: 1.0); wait() times out after 300 s by default and throws JobFailedException (payload on $e->job ) when a job fails. $plan = $cipi->yml()->status('shop')['data']; // file, env, valid, in_sync, changes, blockers foreach ($plan['changes'] as $change) { echo $change['summary'], PHP_EOL; // e.g. "PHP 8.5 → 8.6" } if ($plan['blockers'] === []) { $job = $cipi->jobs()->wait($cipi->yml()->apply('shop'), throwOnFailure: false); $outcome = $job['data']['result']['outcome']; // applied, unchanged, partial, blocked, invalid, no-file } $cipi->yml()->enableAuto('shop'); With auto-apply on, anyone who can commit can change the app's aliases, PHP settings, limits, workers, deploy recipe, schedule, databases and backups. Ask for confirmation before enabling it for someone. Reads need yml-view , writes yml-manage .

$cipi->aliases()->add('shop', 'www.shop.example.com'); $cipi->www()->forceToRoot('shop'); $cipi->redirects()->set('shop', 'https://example.com', 301, keepPath: true); $cipi->redirects()->add('shop', '/blog/', 'https://blog.example.com', 301, true); $cipi->proxies()->add('shop', prefix: '/api/', upstream: 'http://127.0.0.1:3000', stripPrefix: true); $cipi->ssl()->install('shop'); $cipi->ssl()->install('shop', dns: 'cloudflare', account: 'prod', wildcard: true); $cipi->ssl()->setDnsAccount($cloudflareToken, 'prod'); // sync, never returned Redirects and proxies are tested with nginx -t and reverted on failure; the proxy loopback guard can't be bypassed. Laravel Cloud is the Laravel team's fully-managed deployment platform — a Platform-as-a-Service that runs your application on dedicated AWS infrastructure with one-click autoscaling, managed databases (MySQL / serverless Postgres), Valkey cache, object storage, an edge network with DDoS protection, automatic SSL, and scale-to-zero compute. You connect a Git provider, pick a repo, and deploy in under 60 seconds — with no servers to manage. It is the opposite end of the spectrum from Cipi: where Cipi gives you full ownership of a VPS you control, Cloud abstracts the server away entirely in exchange for a usage-based bill. Where Cipi wins: Cost & predictability — Cloud is usage-based: you pay for compute, databases, cache, bandwidth, and storage as you consume them (after the $5 monthly credit). Costs scale with traffic and can be hard to predict. Cipi is free for every server you own, for life — your only cost is the VPS itself, at a fixed, predictable price. You own the server — Cloud runs on infrastructure managed entirely by Laravel on AWS; you never get root, SSH, or control over the underlying machine. Cipi runs on your own VPS at any provider (Hetzner, OVH, DigitalOcean, AWS, bare metal) with full root access and complete control over the stack. No SaaS dependency — Cloud is a hosted platform: if you stop paying, your apps stop running, and management depends on a reachable cloud.laravel.com. Cipi lives entirely on your VPS and works independently of any external service. No vendor lock-in — Cloud ties your deployment, databases, queues, and storage to its managed AWS e

fortrabbit is a managed PHP cloud (Ireland and Virginia) with GitHub deploys, build commands, SSH/SFTP, persistent storage, MySQL, backups, a developer dashboard, plus MCP, CLI, API and agent skills — from about €4.50/month after a 7-day trial. Render is a general-purpose cloud for web services, static sites, workers, cron, Postgres, Redis and Docker — with autoscaling, pull-request preview environments, private networking, a CLI, MCP, and compliance options (SOC 2, HIPAA, ISO 27001). Billing is usage-based. Render treats Laravel as one more service. Cipi is Laravel-first on a native LEMP / Octane stack you control, with no usage invoice and no vendor lock-in. Render wins if you need multi-language deploys, autoscaling, preview apps, or managed data stores without touching a VPS. See the dedicated Cipi vs Render comparison .

20i is a hosting company — reseller plans, managed cloud (20iCloud, AWS, Google Cloud), WordPress, VPS, domains and email — operated through My20i / StackCP, with a free CDN, migrations, 60+ data centers and 24×7 support. They also sell managed Laravel hosting, but the product is a hosting platform, not a Laravel deploy CLI. Cipi does not replace 20i if you need reseller branding, mail, domains or WordPress-at-scale. It replaces 20i when the job is “deploy Laravel on a VPS I already own”: free MIT tooling, Octane, dual MCP, REST API, and no panel lock-in. 20i wins on human support and a full hosting catalog. Sevalla is Kinsta’s application platform: apps, managed databases, S3-compatible object storage and static sites, MCP for agents, 25 data centers and resource-based pricing (no plans). Sevalla wins if you want to drop DIY cloud and keep apps, databases and storage in one managed bill. See the dedicated Cipi vs Sevalla comparison .

Ploi Cloud (ploi.cloud) is a European Laravel/PHP/Node PaaS with memory-based pricing (€13.88/GB), regions in Amsterdam, London and Chicago, git-push deploys, auto-scaling, managed databases, MCP and a CLI. Cipi is a production server provisioner . It is designed to turn a fresh Ubuntu VPS into a live, internet-facing Laravel host — not to run on your laptop, inside a local Docker container, or behind a home NAT. This is explicit in the requirements and is not a bug or missing feature. Cipi needs a server that is: Reachable from the public internet — with a routable public IPv4 address, not hidden behind NAT (home router, corporate firewall, or NAT-only cloud tiers) Running on real hardware or full virtualization (KVM, VMware, Hyper-V, Xen HVM) — not on shared-kernel virtualization (OpenVZ, LXC) or desktop container runtimes that emulate a Linux VM on your machine. Since v5.5.0 the installer detects those and stops with the name of what it found Accessible on ports 22, 80, and 443 — Let's Encrypt HTTP validation, Nginx vhosts, and SSH deploy workflows all assume inbound traffic can reach the host

Cipi is not compatible with local dockerized environments. Tools like Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima, and similar runtimes give you a Linux VM behind NAT on your Mac or Windows machine — no public IP, no inbound routing from the internet, and often a shared kernel under the hood. The Cipi installer may finish, but the result is not a production server: SSL will not work — Certbot cannot complete Let's Encrypt validation when the host is not reachable on port 80 from the internet Domains will not resolve — there is no public endpoint for DNS to point to Deploy and webhook flows break — Git providers, CI runners, and external services cannot reach a NAT-ted local VM Do not install Cipi inside Docker, OrbStack, WSL, or a local VM expecting a working production stack. Use a real VPS — even a €4/month instance is enough for development and staging.

No production server provisioner supports NAT-ted local environments. Commercial panels and open-source tools alike require a public, internet-accessible host — this is how SSL, domain routing, and remote deploy pipelines work. Cipi follows the same rule. The difference is what Cipi does not ask for: no proprietary agent daemon, no dedicated outbound port to an external control panel, and no mandatory cloud account. Cipi runs entirely on your server — you SSH in and use the CLI. The public-internet requirement is about network topology, not about tying you to a SaaS vendor.

For local Laravel development, use Laravel Sail , Laravel Herd , or a plain composer install with php artisan serve . Provision a cheap VPS with Cipi when you need a real staging or production environment.

MariaDB is the default database engine on every Cipi server (port 3306 ). Since v4.8.0 you can also install optional PostgreSQL ( cipi db install pgsql , port 5432 ) and pick an engine per app or database — see cipi db and Why PostgreSQL? . MariaDB remains the right default for most Laravel apps: familiar MySQL-compatible SQL, strong out-of-the-box performance, and a license model that stays simple for self-hosted production.

MariaDB is built for high-concurrency web workloads — exactly the pattern Laravel apps generate (many short queries, connection churn from PHP-FPM, mixed reads and writes). Advanced query optimizer — better join planning and cost-based decisions than classic MySQL for typical application queries, which often means fewer full scans and lower latency under load. Native thread pool — available in the community edition, so the server handles many concurrent connections more efficiently than a one-thread-per-connection model when PHP-FPM spikes. InnoDB tuned for your VPS — Cipi sets innodb_buffer_pool_size from server RAM (256M on 1 GB hosts, up to 4 GB on 16 GB+ machines), so hot data stays in memory without starving Nginx or PHP. Lean default for Laravel — most apps need a fast relational store, not exotic extensions. MariaDB delivers that with low operational overhead on a single Ubuntu box.

Choosing MariaDB avoids the ambiguity that surrounds Oracle MySQL in commercial and redistribution scenarios — especially when you ship products, host client apps, or run infra for a company. Pure GPL community server — MariaDB Server is GPL; there is no dual-license enterprise fork of the core engine that you must navigate just to stay compliant. No Oracle MySQL CLA / dual-license maze — you are not depending on Oracle's MySQL product line, trademark policy, or commercial editions for features that “should” be free. Predictable for SaaS and agencies — self-hosting MariaDB on your VPS keeps database licensing simple: you run open-source software on hardware you control, without MySQL Enterprise feature gates or surprise license reviews. Aligned with Cipi's MIT philosophy — open stack, no vendor lock-in, no paid database SKU required for production performance features like the thread pool.

Drop-in for Laravel — use the mysql driver, the same DB_* env keys, and the same migration files. Eloquent, queues, and most packages just work. Familiar tooling — TablePlus, DBeaver, Sequel Ace, and mariadb / mysql CLI clients connect the same way; Cipi still exposes a ready mariadb+ssh:// URL after install. Native on Ubuntu — installs from MariaDB.org / Ubuntu packaging without inventing a custom database stack; Cipi wires users, backups, and vault credentials on top. Battle-tested for the LAMP/LEMP world — decades of MySQL-compatible applications, docs, and hiring familiarity — with an engine that stays community-first.

Since v4.8.0 , PostgreSQL is a first-class optional engine on Cipi (port 5432 ). Install it with cipi db install pgsql , then create apps or databases with --engine=pgsql — see cipi db . Keep MariaDB as the default for classic Laravel MySQL workloads, or choose Postgres when you need richer SQL, stronger concurrency guarantees, or a stack that grows toward analytics and AI.

Rich SQL and data types — JSON/JSONB, arrays, ranges, UUID, full-text search, and expressive constraints (CHECK, exclusion, deferred FKs) that map cleanly to complex domain models. Powerful indexing — B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, partial and expression indexes — so you can index JSON paths, search documents, or speed up time-series-style queries without a second datastore. Extensions ecosystem — pgcrypto , uuid-ossp , pg_trgm , PostGIS, and many others turn Postgres into a platform, not only a SQL file. First-class Laravel support — native pgsql driver, migrations, Eloquent, and a huge ecosystem of packages that assume Postgres features when you need them.

MVCC done right — readers do not block writers; long-running reports and busy write traffic coexist more gracefully than on lock-heavy setups. Reliable under mixed load — strong consistency, transactional DDL in many cases, and a planner that holds up as schemas and query shapes get more sophisticated. Room to grow on one VPS — then beyond — excellent vertical scale for a single-node Cipi server; when you outgrow the box, the same engine is what managed Postgres, replicas, and logical replication ecosystems are built around. Operational clarity — mature monitoring views ( pg_stat_* ), explain plans, and tooling that senior teams already know how to tune.

Industry standard — Postgres is the default answer for many SaaS backends, analytics pipelines, and cloud “managed database” offerings. Skills and runbooks transfer. Standards-leaning SQL — closer to ANSI SQL than MySQL dialects, which reduces surprise when you share queries across tools, ORMs, and warehouses. Works with the wider data stack — BI tools, ORMs, ETL, and CDC systems almost always speak Postgres; your Cipi-hosted DB is not a dead end. Side-by-side with MariaDB on Cipi — both engines can run on the same server (3306 + 5432). Pick per app: WordPress-style or classic Laravel MySQL on MariaDB; product, multi-tenant, or JSON-heavy apps on Postgres.

h: Ready for AI and modern data workloads
x: Vectors and embeddings — with extensions such as pgvector , you can store embeddings next to relational data for semantic search, RAG, and recommendation features without bolting on a separate vector database on day one. JSONB as a flexible document layer — keep structured columns for invariants and JSONB for evolving AI metadata, model outputs, or tool payloads — queryable and indexable. Full-text + similarity building blocks — combine FTS, trigram similarity, and vectors for hybrid retrieval (keyword + semantic) inside one transactional system. Analytics-friendly — window functions, CTEs, materialized views, and robust aggregation make Postgres a solid home for product metrics and feature stores before you need a warehouse.

Cipi uses Valkey instead of Redis for several reasons: Drop-in replacement — same RESP protocol on port 6379 , same phpredis extension, same REDIS_* .env keys. Laravel doesn't notice the difference. Truly open source — BSD-licensed fork stewarded by the Linux Foundation, created after Redis Inc. moved to the source-available SSPL / RSALv2 in 2024. Native on Ubuntu — ships in Ubuntu 24.04's Universe repository ( valkey-server + valkey-tools ) without third-party PPAs. No vendor lock-in — aligns with Cipi's MIT, self-hosted philosophy: free forever, backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, and a large community. Auto-migrated — existing servers switch from Redis to Valkey automatically on cipi self-update , reusing the same password and dataset with zero app changes.

When v4 was designed, one of the clearest decisions was to drop generic PHP and WordPress support entirely and go all-in on a single framework. That framework was Laravel — and the reasoning goes well beyond personal preference.

Laravel gives developers an extraordinary head start. Authentication, queues, scheduled tasks, file storage, email, notifications, API resources, database migrations — all of it is built in, consistent, and documented. A team can go from an empty project to a production-ready application in a fraction of the time it would take with a lower-level stack. For Cipi, this means that every deployment assumption — directory layout, .env handling, queue workers, the scheduler — maps cleanly to a known structure. There is no guesswork.

Laravel has one of the most active and welcoming communities in the PHP world. Packages are published, maintained, and discussed daily on GitHub, Laracasts, Discord, and X. When you hire a Laravel developer, you get someone who already knows the conventions, the tooling, and the ecosystem. When you publish a Laravel package, it reaches tens of thousands of developers overnight. That network effect is genuinely valuable — and it is one of the reasons Cipi's companion package, cipi-agent , works so well: drop it into a Laravel app and it just fits.

Laravel takes security seriously out of the box. CSRF protection, SQL injection prevention through the query builder, XSS mitigation via Blade's auto-escaping, rate limiting, signed URLs, encrypted cookies — these are not add-ons you wire together, they are the defaults. The framework's release cycle includes prompt security patches, and the team publishes clear upgrade guides. For production applications that handle real users and real data, that reliability matters enormously.

Every major Laravel version receives bug fixes for 18 months and security fixes for two years after release. LTS versions extend that further. Taylor Otwell and the core team have maintained a consistent, principled release cadence since 2011 — a track record that is rare and genuinely reassuring for long-term projects. When you deploy on Cipi, you are not betting on a framework that might be abandoned next year.

Laravel does not stand alone. Around it has grown an ecosystem of first-party and community tools that are among the best in the industry: Livewire — full-stack reactive components without leaving PHP Filament — a stunning admin panel and form builder built on Livewire Inertia.js — the bridge between Laravel and modern front-end frameworks (Vue, React, Svelte) Laravel Horizon — a beautiful dashboard for monitoring Valkey/Redis queues; Cipi enables it with cipi worker horizon enable Laravel Reverb — first-party WebSockets; Cipi wires Supervisor, Nginx /app proxy, and REVERB_* with cipi app reverb enable Laravel Telescope — an elegant debug assistant for local and staging environments Laravel Octane — supercharges application performance with FrankenPHP (and optionally Swoole / RoadRunner). Cipi runs Octane natively: cipi app create --octane or cipi app convert --to=octane Pest — a delightful PHP testing framework with a Laravel-native plugin Laracasts — the best screencasts in PHP, period These tools do not just exist — they are actively developed, widely adopted, and genuinely fun to use. The Laravel world has a rare quality: it manages to be both opinionated enough to feel cohesive and flexible enough to stay out of your way when you need it to.

Taylor Otwell , the founder of Laravel, has a mantra that resonates far beyond the framework: "we must ship." It is a simple statement, but it encapsulates an entire philosophy — that code only has value when it reaches users, that perfectionism is the enemy of progress, and that the best developers are the ones who find ways to move forward even when the conditions are not ideal. The broader tech world has its own, blunter version: ship or die. Build something real, put it in front of people, learn, and iterate — or watch it slowly become irrelevant in a drawer. Laravel's entire ecosystem is built around that spirit. The framework reduces friction, the community celebrates releases, and the tooling rewards velocity. Cipi exists for the same reason: to remove the server management friction that stands between a developer and a live, deployed application. If you are reading these docs, you are probably a developer who wants to build things, not babysit infrastructure. That is exactly the kind of developer Cipi was made for. Cipi is built for Laravel and with Laravel. The installer, the deploy pipeline, the agent package, the cron setup, the worker management — every decision was made with a Laravel app in mind. If you love the framework, you will feel right at home.

Cipi is the Italian reading of the letters C and P — which stand for Control Panel . It is a quiet nod to the project's Italian roots and to the fact that, underneath all the CLI commands, Cipi is doing exactly what a control panel does: managing Nginx, PHP-FPM, MariaDB, Supervisor, Certbot, and UFW on your behalf — just without the browser tab. The name also carries a deliberate lightness. Server management tools tend to take themselves very seriously. Cipi does not. It is a tool built by a developer for developers, with the goal of getting out of the way as quickly as possible.

The Cipi mascot is a penguin — an intentional reference to Tux , the official Linux mascot created by Larry Ewing in 1996. Where Tux is polished and iconic, the Cipi penguin is drawn in a minimal, hand-sketched line style: same species, different attitude. Think of it as Tux's quieter sibling who prefers the terminal over the spotlight. The illustration is rendered as a pure SVG using the project's accent color, so it adapts naturally to light and dark mode and scales to any size without losing quality.

d: From shell scripts in 2019 to Cipi 5.
x: Cipi was created by Andrea Pollastri , a software developer since 2005 specialising in Laravel, system administration, and cybersecurity — with experience at companies like Docebo and Musement. He built Cipi out of a practical need: a fast, scriptable way to provision and deploy Laravel applications on his own VPS, without handing control to a SaaS panel. What started as a private tool became an open-source project that grew to over 1,000 GitHub stars and hundreds of active deployments worldwide. Here is a brief account of how it evolved across six years and five major versions. v0.1 June 2019
A collection of shell scripts to automate the tedious parts of setting up a Laravel server on a fresh Ubuntu VPS — Nginx, PHP, MariaDB, Supervisor. No web UI, no package. Just bash. v1.x June 2019

The shell scripts were wrapped in a Laravel web application acting as a server control panel. Users could create apps, manage deployments, and configure Nginx through a browser UI hosted on the same server. The project was published on GitHub and quickly attracted interest from the Laravel community. v2.x May 2020

A year of rapid iteration added SMTP configuration, local database backups, PHP-FPM permission fixes, server service management, and root password reset. The v2 series reached 2.4.9 across dozens of patch releases, establishing Cipi as a stable option for small-team Laravel hosting. v3.0 March 2021

h: The last web UI — and a question
x: PHP 8.1 became the default version. Node was upgraded to v16, Certbot was refreshed, and domain alias handling was fixed. The v3.1.x series was the most polished release of the web-UI era and many teams kept it running in production for years. It was also the version that prompted a harder question: was a browser-based control panel still the right interface? Modern development workflows had moved toward SSH, CI/CD pipelines, GitOps, and — increasingly — AI agents that could orchestrate infrastructure through shell commands. A web UI required authentication, a running Laravel process, and a database just to issue a deploy. A CLI needed none of that. The answer shaped everything that came next. v4.x March 2026

After years of maintaining a full Laravel web application as the control plane, v4 made the boldest decision yet: drop the web UI entirely . Cipi became a pure CLI tool operated over SSH. The scope also narrowed from generic PHP to Laravel exclusively , allowing every part of the stack to be optimised for one framework. MySQL was replaced by MariaDB 11.4 , git pull was replaced by Deployer zero-downtime releases , shared deploy keys became per-app ed25519 keys, and S3 automated backups and native webhook support for GitHub and GitLab were added from day one. v4 also introduced a complete REST API for programmatic management of hosts and applications, native integration with GitHub and GitLab git providers, a groundbreaking dual MCP server architecture — one per-app and one global — enabling full AI-driven infrastructure management directly from any MCP-compatible IDE or AI agent, encrypted server sync for migrating apps between VPS instances, and a built-in database anonymizer for GDPR-safe data exports. The full v4 changelog is available on GitHub Releases . Keep one alias per server for the cipi admin user and one per app user, instead of remembering hosts and ports. Johnny S3-compatible object storage on your own VPS, powered by Garage and secured by Caddy, with automated backups, a web panel, a CLI and a REST API. Put it on a separate VPS (it brings its own Caddy), then use it as an S3-compatible destination for cipi backup or as a Laravel filesystem disk — off-site, and still on infrastructure you own.

Tool What it does With Cipi Boogle Self-hosted exception tracker and uptime monitor for Laravel: ingests errors from your apps, groups issues, sends digests and watches services. cipi monitor watches the server and cipi health one URL per app; Boogle adds the application view — exceptions and uptime seen from outside. Error payloads stay on your infrastructure. IndieStats Privacy-friendly, self-hosted web analytics on Laravel: real-time dashboards, filters, country map, ASN detection, Excel export — no cookies, no consent banner. A Laravel app like any other: deploy it with cipi app create on a subdomain and track every site on the server without sending visitor data to a third party.

Tool What it does With Cipi Checkpoint Laravel security audit in one Artisan command: known CVEs in dependencies, leaked secrets and injection risks, with CI support and custom checks. Cipi hardens the server; Checkpoint checks the code. Run it in the pipeline before the deploy, so a vulnerable release never reaches the server. Hackly Authorized attack-surface and application security scanning: inventory targets, verify DNS ownership, scan linked GitHub repositories (Laravel/PHP SAST and SCA), review findings in a Filament panel. A continuous vulnerability view across all your projects and domains. Built on Laravel and Filament, so it can run on a Cipi server itself. Its findings sit well next to a cipi compliance report.

Tool What it does With Cipi init One command to scaffold a complete Laravel + Filament local stack on macOS, with Docker, SSL and a real *.127001.it subdomain. Start the project locally with init, push it to Git, and let Cipi take it from there — Git auto-setup , cipi.yml , zero-downtime deploys. Larapilot Spec-driven AI product workflow for Laravel, via Laravel Boost: from product idea to reviewed code, with personas, skills and optional forge and chat notifications. Larapilot shapes the code; the Cipi Agent MCP server and the panel API let the same AI tooling see and operate the running app.
